data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise the Present Perfect for experiences, unfinished time, recent events and situations connected to the present.
learningPoints: Use have/has + past participle to form the Present Perfect.
Use the tense for past experiences when the exact time is not stated.
Use for and since with situations continuing to the present.
Use already, yet, just, ever and never naturally.
Distinguish the Present Perfect from the Past Simple.
Recognise when a past event has a present result.

sections.summary: Using the Present Perfect for life experience.
sections.explain: Use the Present Perfect when talking about experience without saying exactly when it happened.

words.word: I have visited Rome twice.
I visited Rome twice in my life ever.
I have visit Rome twice.

sections.explain: Use SINCE with the point when a continuing situation began.

words.word: She has lived here since 2022.
She has lived here for 2022.
She lived here since 2022 and still does.

sections.summary: Using 'for' with a period of time.
sections.explain: Use FOR with a duration of time.

words.word: We have known each other for ten years.
We have known each other since ten years.
We knew each other for ten years and still do.

sections.explain: JUST commonly appears between HAVE/HAS and the past participle.

words.word: He has just finished his lunch.
He just has finish his lunch.
He has just finish his lunch.

sections.explain: YET is commonly used in Present Perfect questions and negatives about expected events.

words.word: Have you finished your homework yet?
Did you finished your homework yet?
Have you finish your homework yet?

sections.explain: ALREADY often comes between HAVE/HAS and the past participle.

words.word: They have already seen that film.
They already have saw that film.
They have already saw that film.

sections.summary: Using Present Perfect with unfinished time.
sections.explain: Use the Present Perfect when the time period is still continuing, such as TODAY or THIS WEEK.

words.word: I have had three meetings today.
I had three meetings today, and today is not finished.
I have have three meetings today.

sections.summary: Using Past Simple with a finished past time.
sections.explain: Use the Past Simple when a finished past time is stated.

words.word: I saw her yesterday.
I have seen her yesterday.
I have saw her yesterday.

sections.summary: Using Present Perfect for a present result.
sections.explain: Use the Present Perfect when a recent past action has an important result now.

words.word: I've lost my keys, so I can't open the door.
I lost my keys, so I can't open the door now, ever.
I've lose my keys, so I can't open the door.

sections.summary: Using 'ever' in a Present Perfect question.
sections.explain: EVER is commonly used in questions about experience.

words.word: Have you ever eaten Korean food?
Did you ever eaten Korean food?
Have you ever ate Korean food?
